cards.title: LangChain is the bricks. LangGraph is the wiring.
cards.body: LangChain gives an LLM memory, tools and the ability to do things in sequence. LangGraph decides *who does what, in what order, and what happens when something goes wrong*. You don't pick one — LangGraph is built on top of LangChain.
cards.why: Every architecture decision you make starts with: is this a straight line (chain) or does it need to loop and branch (graph)?

diagram.caption: LangChain: A → B → C, no loops

cards.title: State is the relay baton.
cards.body: Every node picks up the State, does its work, and passes it on. Nodes never talk to each other directly — they only read from and write to State. That's why a LangGraph graph is easy to debug: look at the baton between steps.

cards.title: Why does chunk_overlap exist?

quiz.question: You split a PDF into 1000-char chunks with chunk_overlap=200. What does the overlap buy you?
options: Faster embedding because chunks share text
Context that straddles a chunk boundary isn't lost
quiz.explain: If chunk 1 ends mid-sentence, the 200 chars of overlap mean chunk 2 still carries that sentence. Without it, the answer to a question can be sliced in half and neither chunk retrieves well.

cards.title: The docstring IS the tool description.
cards.body: With `@tool`, the LLM never sees your Python. It sees the function name, the argument types and the docstring. A vague docstring = a tool that gets called at the wrong time, or never.
cards.why: Most 'my agent won't use the tool' bugs are docstring bugs.

cards.title: ReAct = Reason, Act, Observe, repeat.
cards.body: The agent writes a thought, picks a tool, reads the result, and loops until it decides it has an answer. In LangGraph this is literally a cycle: `agent → tools → agent`, with a conditional edge that exits when there are no more tool calls.

diagram.caption: The loop that makes it an agent

cards.title: A checkpointer turns a graph into something that can pause.
cards.body: Add `checkpointer=MemorySaver()` (or Postgres in prod) and every node's output is saved per `thread_id`. That gives you: resume after a crash, multi-turn memory, time-travel debugging, and human-in-the-loop interrupts.

code.src:
graph = builder.compile(
    checkpointer=MemorySaver(),
    interrupt_before=["send_email"],
)
config = {"configurable": {"thread_id": "user-42"}}
graph.invoke(state, config)   # pauses before send_email
graph.invoke(None, config)    # resumes after approval

cards.why: Checkpoint history is also your audit log — this is why regulated teams pick LangGraph.

cards.title: Supervisor + workers.
cards.body: One supervisor node reads State and routes to a specialist (researcher, coder, writer). Each worker does its job and returns control to the supervisor, which decides: another worker, or END.

diagram.caption: Conditional edge from supervisor picks the worker

cards.title: LangSmith vs DeepEval — who does what?

quiz.question: You want tracing AND RAG quality tests without the two fighting. Which split keeps it clean?
options: LangSmith for traces, DeepEval in pytest for faithfulness/relevancy — never enable DeepEval's tracer
Both tracers on, compare the dashboards
LangSmith evals only, DeepEval is redundant
quiz.explain: Separate lanes: LangSmith sees every run live; DeepEval scores a small golden set on demand. Two tracers at once doubles the noise and the API keys.

cards.title: One line of MLflow for agent traces.
cards.body: If you already live in MLflow for data work, you don't need a new observability tool to start. Autolog hooks LangChain's callback system and shows each chain/tool call as a span in the UI you already know.

code.src:
import mlflow
mlflow.langchain.autolog()

with mlflow.start_run():
    result = graph.invoke({"question": q}, config)

cards.title: The pipe is just function composition.
cards.body: `prompt | llm | parser` builds a Runnable. Each `|` passes the output of the left into the input of the right — exactly like a Unix pipe. Everything in LCEL is a Runnable, so a whole chain can be one step inside a bigger chain, or one node inside a graph.

code.src:
chain = prompt | llm | StrOutputParser()
chain.invoke({"topic": "vector DBs"})

# batch and stream come free
chain.batch([{"topic": "RAG"}, {"topic": "agents"}])

cards.title: Send() — the map step of map-reduce in LangGraph.
cards.body: A conditional edge can return a *list* of `Send(node, payload)` objects. LangGraph then runs that node once per payload, in parallel, and a reducer on State merges the results. This is how deep-research agents fan out to N searchers.
cards.why: Your AIgram generator will use exactly this: one planner, fifty parallel writers.

cards.title: Reducers decide how parallel writes merge.
cards.body: When two nodes write the same State key at once, LangGraph needs a rule. `Annotated[list, operator.add]` means append. Without a reducer, the last writer wins — or you get an InvalidUpdateError.

cards.title: interrupt() pauses from *inside* a node.
cards.body: `interrupt_before` pauses at a node boundary. `interrupt(payload)` pauses mid-node, surfaces the payload to a human, and resumes with their answer via `Command(resume=...)`. Use it for approvals, clarifying questions, and 'are you sure?' gates.

cards.title: Checkpoints are short-term. Store is long-term.
cards.body: A checkpointer remembers *this thread*. The `BaseStore` (InMemoryStore, PostgresStore) remembers *across* threads — user preferences, facts, past decisions — keyed by namespace. Nodes get it via the `store` argument.
cards.why: Thread memory vs cross-thread memory is a very common interview question.

cards.title: Faithfulness vs answer relevancy.

quiz.question: Your RAG answer is fluent and on-topic but states a date that isn't in any retrieved chunk. Which metric drops?
quiz.explain: Faithfulness checks whether every claim is supported by the retrieved context. Relevancy only asks whether the answer addresses the question — a hallucinated date can still be perfectly relevant.

cards.title: Vectors miss exact tokens. BM25 misses meaning. Use both.
cards.body: Embedding search fails on part numbers, error codes and names (`ORD-12345`, `E0421`). Keyword search fails on paraphrase. Hybrid retrieval runs both and fuses the rankings (Reciprocal Rank Fusion). Most production RAG is hybrid.

cards.title: Prompts are code. Version them like code.
cards.body: MLflow's prompt registry (`mlflow.genai.register_prompt`) and LangSmith's prompt hub both give you: a version number, a diff, and the ability to pin production to v7 while you test v8. A prompt edited in a notebook and not committed is a silent production change.

code.src:
import mlflow
mlflow.genai.register_prompt(
    name="rag-answer",
    template="Answer using only: {{context}}\nQ: {{question}}",
)
p = mlflow.genai.load_prompt("prompts:/rag-answer@production")

cards.title: with_structured_output() beats parsing JSON by hand.
cards.body: Give the model a Pydantic class and LangChain uses the provider's native tool-calling/JSON mode to return a validated object. No regex, no 'please respond in JSON' begging, and a typed State field at the other end.

code.src:
class Verdict(BaseModel):
    is_duplicate: bool
    reason: str

critic = llm.with_structured_output(Verdict)
v: Verdict = critic.invoke(card_text)

cards.why: Your AIgram critic node is exactly this.

cards.title: This feed is a LangGraph graph.
cards.body: Planner reads your profile and picks ~50 topics across reinforce / next / fresh. A Send() fan-out writes one card per topic in parallel. A critic with structured output rejects duplicates and shallow cards. The survivors become tomorrow's JSON.
cards.why: Every concept in today's deck is a node in the thing that made today's deck.

cards.title: Which LangGraph feature powers the writers?

quiz.question: Fifty cards need writing in parallel from one planner. Which primitive does that?
quiz.explain: Send() returns one unit of work per topic; LangGraph schedules them concurrently and a reducer appends the results. A for-loop of add_edge would run them in sequence.
